# When a gene total is the wrong unit

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Assembled from the claim records the earlier chapters were written from, and not
yet reviewed by a second reader. It introduces no source and no number that is
not already stated in full somewhere earlier in the book.
:::

Every chapter so far has argued the same proposition one study at a time, and
none of them has added the figures up. That is the fault this book charges the prevalence figure with in
@sec-how-functional, so it is worth not repeating.
The two tables below put the quantities side by side with the unit each one was
measured in.

They are tables rather than a chart on purpose. The rows do not share a denominator, so there is no axis they can all sit on. A
bar chart would invite the comparison the numbers cannot support.

## Isoform effects with no gene-level signal {#sec-the-tally}

Each row gives a figure exactly as its source states it, what that figure
counts, and the section where the result is stated in full, and nothing in it is averaged or
pooled.

| Figure | What it counts | Assay | Home | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 42 to 46 per cent | genes called as isoform switches that showed no gene-level difference | bulk short read, Barrett's progression | @sec-invisible-switches | [@zhang2022esophageal] |
| 49 of 229 | isoform pairs separating two breast subtypes with no gene-level difference | bulk short read, TCGA | @sec-invisible-switches | [@zhao2016switching] |
| roughly a quarter | tumour-side transcripts differentially used but not differentially expressed | bulk short read, twelve TCGA types | @sec-invisible-switches | [@dolgalev2023switching] |
| about seven in ten | genes carrying isoform variation not explained by the gene's own expression | single-cell long read, brain | @sec-isoform-only | [@joglekar2024singlecell] |
| about a third | cases of differing isoform proportions with no significant change in gene total | single-cell long read, cross-tissue | @sec-isoform-only | [@mantri2026splice], preprint |
| about half | isoforms differentially expressed in a cluster whose gene was also differentially expressed | single-cell long read, CD8 T cells | @sec-isoform-only | [@tzaban2025rna], preprint |
| about a tenth | differential three-prime UTR events that coincide with a change in the gene's expression | 3'-end single cell, 474 cell types | @sec-sc-apa | [@fansler2024quantifying] |
| 70.6 per cent | isoform-level expression QTLs absent from the gene-level list on the same reads | nanopore long read, 67 B cell lines | @sec-gtex-lr | [@nagura2025longread] |
| a fifth | cis associations on isoform-to-gene ratios with no significant gene-level association | short read, Framingham whole blood | @sec-isoform-qtl | [@liu2025integrating] |

Two rows point the opposite way from the rest and are easy to misread. The
Fansler figure is the share of three-prime UTR events that *do* coincide with an
expression change, so it is the small number that makes the point. The Tzaban
figure is the share that *was* also visible at gene level, so again the
remainder is the claim.

The configuration that makes a gene total actively misleading is narrower than
any of these rows. In the B cell data, 1,135 variants had significantly
different effect sizes on different isoforms of one gene and 153 pushed two
isoforms in opposite directions [@nagura2025longread]. Summing isoform counts
into a gene total cancels that second group exactly, and no amount of depth
recovers it.

## The deflationary results {#sec-the-other-side}

The deflationary results are scattered across the book in the same way, and
collecting them is the only honest way to read the table above.

| Figure | What it counts | Assay | Home | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.12 | expressed transcripts per gene, averaged | bulk short read, primary tissues | @sec-scale | [@gonzalezporta2013dominanttranscript] |
| roughly 85 per cent | protein-coding mRNA coming from each gene's major transcript | bulk short read, primary tissues | @sec-how-functional | [@gonzalezporta2013dominanttranscript] |
| about 2,000 | alternatively spliced exons predicted conserved between human and mouse | EST-era comparison | @sec-how-functional | [@conservedas2005humanmouseexons], abstract only |
| 13.9 against 2.8 per cent | heritability explained by the expression-QTL and splicing-QTL annotations | SBayesRC on blood | @sec-how-much | [@liu2025transcriptional], preprint |
| 32 against 4 per cent | repression of stability and of translation by the strongest three-prime UTR element | one mouse cell line | @sec-utr-only | [@spies2013utrisoform] |
| two of 7 and two of 36 | patients reaching one interval of eight-week transfusion independence | phase 1 dose expansion | @sec-cancer-therapeutics | [@h3b8800phase1lrmds2025], abstract only |

One result belongs here and carries no number. An annotation-free analysis of two large mouse single-cell atlases found
splicing strongly tied to cell identity. In those authors' hands it never
revealed a cell subpopulation that expression clustering had missed
[@benegas2022robust]. The positive case for
isoform data finding new populations rests on one monocyte split
[@olivieri2021splicing], and @sec-sc-structure gives both sides.

## Choosing the unit for an analysis {#sec-the-rule}

The tables do not resolve into a single fraction, and a reader looking for one
should stop here. What they support is narrower and more useful, which is a set
of conditions under which a gene total is the wrong unit.

A gene total is the wrong unit when two isoforms move in opposite directions,
because the sum is unchanged by construction and the effect cannot be recovered
downstream. It is the wrong unit when the question is which protein the gene makes.
Start-site and terminal-exon choice reach the protein ends far more often than
internal splicing does, as @sec-what-changes sets out. It is the
wrong unit when the isoform carries the regulatory elements rather than the
coding sequence, which is the three-prime UTR case of @sec-utr-only. And it is
the wrong unit when the phenotype is a ratio held between two forms, as
@sec-mapt shows for tau.

A gene total is defensible, and often preferable, in the ordinary case. Most
genes express about one transcript, one transcript carries most of the output,
and most annotated splicing is unconserved and probably inconsequential. Those
three statements are the subject of @sec-how-functional and they have not been
overturned by anything in the chapters since.

Between those two sets sits the decision that actually matters, which is which
null hypothesis a study is testing. @sec-dtu separates total output, isoform composition and individual transcript
abundance into three different questions. Most of the disagreement collected
above is really a disagreement about which of the three a given number answers.

## Limits on reading the two tables {#sec-the-gap}

Three gaps are worth stating plainly, because each one bounds how far the
tables above can be taken.

The fractions cannot be combined with each other. They count genes, isoform
pairs, transcripts, events, QTLs and associations, measured on different assays
in different tissues. The leads behind @sec-isoform-qtl record explicitly that
they must not be averaged. Anyone wanting one number for how much isoform biology matters
will have to define the denominator first, and that choice will do more work
than the data.

The protein layer is thinner than the RNA layer. @sec-is-it-translated gets as far as showing that a well-covered gene's
alternative products are seen about as often as its main one. @sec-measuring
explains why confirming a particular proteoform in a particular tissue remains a
targeted experiment.

Several of the strongest figures above are preprints or abstracts. The table
marks each one, and `research/ALLOCATION.md` lists every source in the book
whose provenance is weaker than its DOI suggests. A number from a preprint is
not wrong, and it is not yet checked by anyone outside the group that produced
it.
